title: Northgate Week
part: PART FOUR: THE OTHER KIND OF CONFIDENCE

pages.text:
*Way to Lose #47: Meet the other team's star and decide to hate him.*

The Northgate Wolves arrive in a bus that has a bathroom. I know because I counted the windows, and one of them has a small sign that says Restroom, which is an insult to my bladder. They step out in matching white and blue uniforms, polished so they shine. They look like a commercial for a toothpaste.

Josie is standing on the sidelines with her clipboard. She reads their stats aloud. "Kai Brandt, twelve goals, three assists, zero fouls. Their keeper has a 98% save percentage. Their midfield averages 4.2 passes per minute."

Tank puts his hand over her mouth. "Josie," he whispers. "Could you read something a little less loud? My ears are ringing."

Josie pulls his hand away. "It is just data, Tank. Data is neutral. Data does not have a volume knob."

Coach Gin walks up to the bus. She looks at the vehicle, then at the polished shoes of the first Wolf to step off. She takes a sip from her steel thermos.

"Nice bus," she says. Her voice is flat. She does not sound impressed. Nor afraid. She sounds like she is commenting on the weather.

The Wolves do not know how to handle a coach who is not intimidated. They just stand there, holding their sticks, looking very confused. I feel a weird little spark in my chest. It is not fear. It is something else. I do not have a name for it yet.
pages.image: A bright big blank yellow minibus with a restroom sign parked on a grassy field; a small silver-haired woman in a yellow windbreaker stands calmly in front of it, holding a thermos, while a group of polished kids in white and blue uniforms look confused.

pages.text:
I go to the Dugout Diner to think. The milkshakes here are thick enough to stand a spoon in, provided the spoon is very strong and very desperate. I sit in a booth with cracked vinyl seats and try to work out what I am feeling. It is not excitement, and it is not dread. It is a tightness in my throat, like I swallowed a marble.

A boy sits in the booth next to me. He wears a white and blue warm-up top, spotless, with a plain hamburger in front of him. No fries, no ketchup, just meat and bun. He looks like a person who has been told exactly what to eat, and when, and how many bites per minute.

He looks at me. He knows who I am. Everyone knows who I am now, because the video is everywhere. It is on every phone, every laptop, and probably every smart fridge in the county.

"Kai Brandt," I say, trying to sound tough. I fail.

He shrugs. "I watched the own goal," he says, his voice quiet. "I have done that. In fifth grade. Nobody filmed it. Lucky."
pages.image: A diner booth with cracked red vinyl; a wiry girl with a high ponytail and yellow armband sits across from a boy in a white and blue top eating a plain hamburger; a tall water glass sits between them on the table.

pages.text:
We talk for twenty minutes, and I have absolutely no idea how to stop the conversation. He tells me about his dad, Coach Brandt, who is not exactly a villain but is certainly a man with a clipboard and a voice loud enough to rattle the diner windows.

"Every game," Kai says, picking at a single crumb on the table. "Every single one. If we win, it is because I executed the plan. If we lose, I have to explain why I did not."

He looks down at his plain hamburger. "I have not had a game in two years that I did not have to explain at dinner. My mom asks, 'Did you hold the line, Kai?' And I have to say yes. Even if I did not."

I look at him. He looks tired, the kind of tired that comes from holding your breath for a long time. His eyes are dark, and he keeps rubbing the spot on his wrist where his watch used to be.

"You guys look like you are having fun," he says. He looks at me like I have just told him that gravity works differently on Earth, or that homework is optional on Tuesdays.

"We are," I say.

He nods. He does not believe me, but he does not argue, which I guess is a start.
pages.image: Two kids sitting in a diner booth, the boy in the white and blue top looking tired and resting his chin on his hand, the girl in the yellow armband looking at him with an open expression; a plain hamburger sits on the table between them.

pages.text:
The door slams open with a bang that makes the coffee in my cup jump. A man steps in. He wears a white polo shirt and dark pants, a whistle dangling around his neck. His face looks like it has never smiled in public. His eyes scan the room and lock onto Kai.

The noise of the coffee machines and clattering plates drops away. It is just the hum of the fridge and the silence of everyone pretending not to look.

"Kai," the man says. His voice is short and hard. It hits the walls and comes back. "It is time to go."

Kai stands up so fast he knocks over his water glass. It splashes across the table. He does not even notice. His shoulders hunch as he rises, rigid as a board.

"Sorry," he mouths to me.

I look at the water spreading across the table. I understand, suddenly, that his confidence is on loan, too. It is just a different kind of loan. He borrows it from his dad. I used to borrow it from the crowd. We are both just holding it, hoping it does not break.
pages.image: A man in a white polo shirt standing rigidly in a diner aisle, looking sternly at a boy in a white and blue top who is standing up abruptly; water is spilling from a glass on the table next to the boy.

pages.text:
Friday night. The last practice before the game. The field is dark, lit by floodlights that buzz like angry bees. The team is gathered in a circle, nobody saying anything as we wait for the speech.

Coach Gin steps forward. She has no whistle in her mouth and no clipboard in her hand. Instead, she holds a single sheet of paper. It is white and clean.

She hands it to me. I take it. I look down.

There are only three words on the top line, printed in a simple, black font.

Play the game.

Underneath that, in tiny writing that is almost too small to see, is one more line.

The scoreboard is not invited.

I look up at Gin. She is drinking her tea, not looking at me but at the field. She looks like a lake. I fold the paper and put it in my sock, right next to the card. It feels heavy. It feels real. I am ready.
pages.image: A dark soccer field under bright floodlights; a small silver-haired woman in a yellow windbreaker stands facing a group of kids in red jerseys, holding a white piece of paper; a girl in the foreground looks down at the paper in her hand.
